speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the Budget Statement debate, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister painted a mixed outlook going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Major economies like US and EU are seeing slower growth and may enter into recession.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The war in Ukraine may escalate or prolong, which could further weigh on global trade, hold up energy and food prices and dampened consumer and business confidence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The bright spark is the reopening of the China economy, which could boost demand for the global economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the intense rivalry and competition between major powers has led to countries taking unilateral actions to decouple in trade, technology, finances and investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To shore up their economic security, we have seen countries like US introduced the Chips Act; and China implemented the Export Control Law to reduce dependencies on other countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Domestically, Singapore is also running up against serious internal resource constraints; among others the ageing resident workforce, rising wages, decarbonisation, high rental and land costs, higher taxes among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How do we stay competitive and how should our businesses prepare for these challenges?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The proliferation of disruptive technologies such as AI, blockchain, Web3 are expected to have uneven impact across businesses; with some embracing the changes and others falling behind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The global shifts towards renewable energy are another challenge that businesses must contend with.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The journey to transit to low or zero carbon is expected to be a taxing one for businesses especially the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides higher carbon taxes, the immediate impact would be the initial higher energy costs and the additional resources needed for the shift.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Next, comes the manpower crunch that businesses faced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding layoffs in the tech sector, the labour market continues to tighten.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The turnover of foreign labour, where the experienced workers go on home leave whilst the newer inexperienced workers take on, add to the tightness of the manpower situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am also concern about the overdrive mode of our domestic economy, especially in the service sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It would further squeeze to the limited manpower availability and drive up costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Improving productivity and efficient utilisation of resources are the only way out to create new capacity for further growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The ITMs are our main playbook to improve productivity and to press on with innovations and internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for an update on our industry transformation efforts so far?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under this vision, there are four key pillars identified which would drive new growth, namely services, manufacturing, trade and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our handling of the pandemic and the balanced approach that we have taken has lifted our credentials.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are the early movers to reinstate air travel which helps to strengthen our air hub status and our premier status as an international convention centre.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Investors see attractiveness in our overall economic proposition and are even prepared to pay the premium to invest or hub in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will create new job opportunities and new economic value add.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Credit goes to EDB, MTI and the other agencies for continuing to attract quality investments to Singapore despite the intense competition and more challenging circumstance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We would need to sharpen our competitive edge to attract and retain investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how he sees the impact to our attractiveness as an investment destination with this move?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Global Enterprises Initiative and the SME co-investment fund are targeted to support and help businesses scale up and be globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how are we supporting our firms to capture opportunities from the region and other emerging markets?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, what steps is Singapore taking to strengthen our trade, economic and digital linkages with other economic partners?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it is always a better position having to deal with the problems of success than to deal with problems of failures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately for us, we are in a position to build on our past successes and strengths to secure an exciting future for all of us in the new era.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last year, MTI announced our Singapore Economy 2030 vision across four key pillars of Services 2030, Trade 2030, Manufacturing 2030 and Enterprise 2030.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are challenging targets considering the economic conditions and headwinds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global unemployment is expected to rise by millions both this year and next, which may force countries to become more protectionist.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Soaring interest rates discourage investments into R&D and training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also not forgetting the phased carbon tax and measures that will be coming in force to secure Singapore's longer-term future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on our progress towards the four key pillars of Singapore Economy 2030?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Based on prevailing investment trends, can I see the Minister's crystal ball or trend forecast in terms of how will the structure of the Singapore economy evolve over the next decade?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does it create jobs, disrupt potential jobs and set the tone for our future generations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The National Productivity Fund was established in 2010 and has been instrumental in driving productivity in Singapore's businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we expand the scope of the fund to anchor more quality investments into Singapore, how do we ensure that the funds are effectively used by businesses to drive real productivity improvements that will lower the cost of doing business in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, the cost of doing business in Singapore is continuously rising.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially due to the rising cost of labour which can be attributed to the tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Aspiration of workforce to have higher pay each year and our collective desire to pay our lower-wage workers better through the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our strong currency also means Singapore-based businesses are finding it harder to compete through costs in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, additional headwind such as the impending carbon tax and the implementation of base erosion and profit-sharing BEPS 2.0 Initiative, would add even more cost to doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While businesses in Singapore face these pressures, in the meantime, the US and other countries are rolling out subsidies to build up their industries and hence, reduce Singapore's attractiveness for investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As tax equalisation in BEPS 2.0 also implies that we have one less instrument to assist us in attracting investments into Singapore, how can we generate non-tax incentives to enhance our business competitiveness to continue to attract foreign investments when we lose preferential tax rates as one of our competitive levels?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These range from technology to monitor health conditions at home, to senior-friendly food, to robotic pet dogs that keep lonely seniors mentally and emotionally engaged.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is one of the most rapidly ageing societies in the world and faces a manpower shortage in the care sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While various agencies such as the MOH, GovTech and IMDA have led the way in certain areas, can more be done to collaborate with the private sector and encourage local enterprises and startups to expand into such technology?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is some evidence that the testing and tailoring of aged care innovations could bring about profits for local businesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, a Singaporean-based company called SilverActivities designs and evaluates games, applications and devices suited primarily for seniors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Their products are designed to stimulate, train and preserve the seniors' cognitive functions such as memory, problem-solving, language and learning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nursing homes have given glowing testimonials of their products.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Companies such as SilverActivities have the potential to expand out into international markets when the time is right.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Market opportunities were identified to be in telemedicine, healthtech, elderly nutrition and assisted living.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are opportunities for Singapore to pioneer, pilot and grow silver industry players that may in time export these goods and services to other countries facing the same demographic challenge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How is the Government catalysing the potential of the Silver Economy?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, it was evident during the global panic in the earlier phases of the pandemic that Singapore has to be self-reliant with resources to combat and resist the spread of the next wave of infectious diseases, and that it is important to have a strong biotech and biomedical industry of our own.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our efforts to promote and grow the sector have been in place since 2000.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we have seen increases in manufacturing value add and growth in jobs in the sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The sector also was a bright spot during the economic hard times of the pandemic years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also the case that the Government has invested a lot in the sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The sector does well when it comes to manufacturing, although commentators have said that there is room for improvements for innovation capability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in spite of this view, some of our biotech enterprises are doing promising, innovative work in interesting areas.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, as Singaporeans, we are proud of our food heritage and it seems a match made in heaven for our companies to focus on what is going into our bodies and how our bodies react to what we consume.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The gut microbiome is neglected at our own peril, as it has also been found to play important roles in regulating our immune systems and controlling brain health and function.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This field therefore appears to hold promise when it comes to providing insight tailored to the specificities of a population and has implications for more efficient use of our resources in our health efforts, from developing effective preventive health strategies to managing or minimising chronic illness, to having more tailored and accurate public education advice when it comes to dietary habits suited to the genetics of our mostly Asian population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The work is cutting edge and is especially cogent in light of the launch of Healthier SG last year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would also make sense to have such knowledge and input be taken on board into our public health systems in an age of rising health and other care costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are our systems sufficiently set up to be able to support such companies to be able to first secure the necessary funding to first research, then develop and market cutting edge products for us to export to the rest of the world?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On accessible support for small businesses, it is an economically difficult time especially for small and micro-businesses as they battle rising costs and inflation amongst other global headwinds in the wake of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, these businesses would also be particularly hard hit by our green transformation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it might sometimes melt into the background as other more pressing and tangible economic concerns take precedence, its impact and undercurrents do not go away.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Small and micro-businesses will soon feel the trickle-down effects of increased environmental regulations and pressures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is important that sufficient and flexible support is provided for them to build capacity on sustainability matters in these times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is also, as Senior Minister of State Teo mentioned last week, that we will be enhancing our public procurement strategy, to take into account public sector sustainability efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our small and micro-businesses should not feel confused or overwhelmed by the diverse schemes and other support options available to them with the attendant KPIs and targets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, could the Government introduce a variety of nudges and incentives to encourage small businesses to more quickly integrate sustainability, in particular environmental sustainability, into their businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to ask how the Government has taken steps to ensure that access to funding and support to navigate and successfully apply for green financing schemes are provided.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Enterprise Sustainability programme can also be expanded to include support to access sustainable financing opportunities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sustainability should be a driving focus of innovation and economic resilience and the Government is a key enabler to making this core to our small businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During last year's debate, during the Second Reading of the Carbon Pricing (Amendment Bill), my Sengkang colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and I both spoke about the need for an EXIM bank and the role that such a bank can play in our efforts to assist our homegrown businesses, in particular our SMEs, internationalise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially important as our domestic economy has natural limits due to our small size.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To address concerns about an EXIM bank turning into something akin to an aid agency, exposures to overseas customers could also be managed by lending to a borrower and having the borrower provide vendor financing to its international customers, as a borrower would be more familiar with the market in which it operates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has limited options when it comes to sustainable energy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our green financing needs would quite naturally be cross-border in nature.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also provide some level of security to businesses by being the lender on record rather than have naturally higher-risk private banks or financial institutions be lenders through difficult times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An EXIM bank can also play a part in developing and exporting green standards by being a sustainable lender or a ranger for capital market instruments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means the EXIM bank would have full direct information about sustainability-related covenants and information on lenders and issuers to which they issue their products or lend funds to.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many Singapore SMEs faced significant challenges.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For most, the pandemic has led to a significant decrease in demand for many products and services which has resulted in a decline in revenue.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They faced cash flow problems and find it difficult to meet their financial obligations, pay employees and invest in the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This was especially so for those with high rental costs and depend mainly on physical stores and delivery.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The supply chain disruptions were severe and many could not access the resources and materials they need to operate.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For many others, finished products could not be shipped or distributed.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Most SMEs were not equipped for remote work.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There were challenges communicating, coordinating and managing the businesses which led to problems with productivity and reliability of service.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is especially so for those who have not embarked on their digital transformation to complete their sales and marketing online.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Businesses face several difficulties especially when operating costs are rising faster than expected with a higher inflation environment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As costs increase, businesses may need to raise prices to maintain their profit margins.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, there is usually a lag in price adjustments especially for those in the contract manufacturing or with ongoing or unfulfilled contracts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The cost of goods and operating costs continues to rise but these companies continue to face outstanding obligations leading to reduced profit margins.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Under such circumstances, many companies will face cash flow problems which is further exacerbated by higher borrowing costs and a tighter credit market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In a tightened financial market, businesses will have difficulty accessing financing especially those with high levels of debt or have a poor credit rating.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, what can businesses do to adapt to rising operating costs and tightened financial markets and what will the Government do to help them?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, our SMEs continue to navigate a challenging environment including rising costs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Locally, the GST increase would also impact smaller SMEs who are not GST-registered and a higher CPF salary ceiling announced in this Budget will add further pressures to businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, what further measures will MTI provide to support SMEs and encourage them to adapt in such a challenging environment?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I have received feedback from SMEs welcoming Deputy Prime Minister’s response during the Budget debate, where he said that agencies will continue to streamline and improve the application process for Government assistance schemes, balancing convenience and accountability.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this point, can MTI share more details on what refinements to the existing administrative processes for Government schemes are being considered?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be more forums for SMEs to provide further feedback?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we would all agree that the Job Support Scheme, SGUnited Jobs and Skills, Enterprise Financing Scheme and other COVID-19 measures have helped our businesses tide over the difficult COVID-19 years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have after close to three years emerged from COVID-19 but unfortunately, we have to now deal with escalating food and energy prices and high inflationary pressures.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our companies are struggling with high business costs and manpower challenges.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While the extension of the Enterprise Financing Scheme (EFS) and Energy Efficiency Grants (EFG) will help businesses sustain, many may not be able to afford to invest to build their business for the future because of the high interest rates.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can Government encourage our financial services ecosystem to support our SMEs to still invest in their businesses for the future?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With Budget 2023, it is clear that the Government is moving away from “handouts” to a Budget that “invests to build for growth, sustainability and resilience”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will however require companies to drive change like job redesign, digitalisation, automation, reskilling and so on, and change is hard work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is likened to many of us trying to get fit and learning to use “new muscles” and new diets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will take time but to do this, we must.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is the foundation to staying healthy and competitive.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If driving productivity is hard work, transformation and innovation is even more hard work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will take leadership at the very top to make it happen.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged to hear the story of Jumain Sataysfaction, a Singapore food manufacturer whose bosses had an “a-ha!” moment when they participated in the Meatless Meat Challenge organised by Singapore Polytechnic’s Food Innovation and Resource Centre (FIRC), Singapore Food Manufacturers' Association (SFMA) and Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They worked closely with the polytechnic students to finalise their concepts for creating a new product range with plant-based options.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Polytechnic (SP) students with their lecturers’ coaching translated the concepts into actual food products with relevant marketing and communication strategies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A new plant-based satay product was created and aptly named "SOVEG".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SOVEG will soon be showcased at the upcoming Gulfood exhibition in Dubai.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But to bring an innovation from creation to the market will take investments.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will MTI facilitate and encourage our Singapore companies to get started in their innovation journey and take it from creation to production to market?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Well, while it is a welcomed move to have the Government to step in to encourage innovation and share risks with SMEs on their innovation journey, there are many business leaders who are sceptical about the take-up rate and the short-term impact as innovation does take time to bear fruit and most SMEs are looking at "today" rather than "tomorrow".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So beyond grants and financial assistance, how else is MTI going to help to develop a strong and vibrant innovation ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We hear too often that Singapore’s market is too small.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our companies highlight uncertainty as the key barrier when internationalising.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The uncertainty of demand, unfamiliarity of business climate and the ability to find suitable partners are some of the issues.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To support Singapore companies with their aspirations to internationalise, Enterprise Singapore (ESG) collaborated with SBF to set up Global-Connect@SBF.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In 2022, Global-Connect@SBF assisted Hot Spicy Mama to sell their products in Qatar and will be helping them to explore other markets in Middle East and South Asia.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond Singapore seems to be the way to go, but for those who are venturing overseas, Budget 2023 seems a little light on internationalisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government provide geopolitical intelligence support for our businesses in their market risk assessment and in navigating the geopolitical challenges as well as facilitating their internationalisation efforts?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, MTI Minister Gan Kim Yong painted the vision of Singapore Economy 2030, refreshed Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs), signed digital economic agreements and green economy agreements to rally our tripartite partners to seize the many opportunities in our turbulent world and stay relevant in the global economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Together, Forward Singapore is the only way to go.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am glad you are referring to the F&B businesses and not something else.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, high inflationary pressures in 2022 have impacted the labour market.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Singapore emerges out of the pandemic, businesses require more manpower to operate at higher levels.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Yet, some businesses we have spoken to, find themselves unable to fill positions for skilled jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses from the manufacturing sector find themselves short of adequate talent, impacting the operations of businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Widespread operational constraints will impact the industry, leading to a decrease in output as they struggle to fill needed jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Operational constraints will also impact our attractiveness to foreign investments and affect Singapore's position on the global value chain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What should businesses do to adapt to the tight labour market and manpower challenges?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With our tight labour market, businesses shared that talent is constantly moving around companies or industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do we help businesses find the appropriate talent to ensure consistent operations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Does their role include working with businesses to align career planning and training to upskill their employees to stay relevant as the businesses transform.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we are able to plan for the reskilling and training of our talent in alignment with the profile of talent required to support the economic opportunities and growth, we will be able to grow a strong talent base and capabilities and provide fulfilling careers for workers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: It is imperative to develop our local leadership and talent.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Local talent has a better understanding of the local market, including customer needs, cultural nuances and regulatory requirements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This can help businesses to better meet the needs of their customers and compete more effectively in the local market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This is especially so in Asia where the diversity of cultures and operating environment vary substantially.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: However, when there is a tight local labour market, businesses will face much difficulty.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: There is a much smaller pool of available candidates, businesses struggle to find workers with the specific skills and experience that they require.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This is further exacerbated when there is an increased competition for talent within a single industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Businesses will have to compete for the same pool of candidates.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: If businesses are unable to fill critical roles or have to rely on inexperienced workers, this can lead to lower productivity and profitability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Eventually, without a sufficient supply of skilled workers, businesses will struggle to expand or take on new projects.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, what can businesses do to adapt to the tighter labour market and manpower challenges?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: What is the Government doing to develop talent locally and preparing them to take on leadership roles and help their companies grow?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question to be asked is what must be done to create the manpower to achieve the vision of Manufacturing 2030.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore gets closer to the world technology frontier, the pace of technological diffusion slows down, thus moderating Singapore's per capita GDP growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It will be the development of indigenous innovation such as the innovative activities and vision in Manufacturing 2030 that shall provide the additional growth to the Singapore economy in its mature phase.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Central to achieving the vision, is the supply of both innovators and workers who make career choices to work in manufacturing.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, what can be done to increase the supply of workers who make career choices to work in manufacturing?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As the standard of living and wealth increase and educational attainments are higher, workers' preferences tend to shift.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There are job tasks that people willingly perform when they are relatively less well-off but which they shun when they are richer.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: An important idea from the assignment model of matching workers' skills and abilities to job tasks, is that a competitive labour market leads workers with different skill sets to be matched with job tasks of different complexities based upon their comparative advantage.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, suppose that workers' job preferences shift for reasons that are unrelated to comparative advantage.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Let us say a job in the financial services sector now becomes more attractive than the job in the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In that case, the size of the economy's total GDP will be suboptimal as people without comparative advantage choose to work in the financial services sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The employment share of the manufacturing sector will then be sub-optimally low, while the employment share of the financial services sector will be sub-optimally high.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What might be done to facilitate the entry of more workers with the aptitude and skills to job tasks in the manufacturing sector?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, what can be done to help increase the supply of innovators?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Factors such as the family environment and exposure to inspiring role models affect the likelihood of an individual to become an innovator.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There could also be intrinsic abilities to innovate that might not be distributed equally among individuals.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: From a policy point of view, what can be done to harness the intrinsic abilities of individuals to innovate from an early age and provide the opportunity for them to develop these talents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Can more scholarships, internships and exposure opportunities be given to students at the different stages of their education ladder to discover whether they have the passion for innovating?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This must be done in conjunction with the different stages of innovation, from basic research to applied stages and on to the marketing of the new products or processes.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Translating inventiveness into the actual flow of ideas requires not just intrinsic talent but also education and training.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is also an issue of access to financial resources that can inhibit innovation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A talented individual who could potentially become a major contributor to creating new ideas that will lead to new products that can be marketed, might be born into a financially constrained family.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What can be done to reach such individuals to help them achieve their potential to contribute to indigenous innovation?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, an integration of all these efforts from the early stages of education to creating new ideas at the workplace will help to develop the country as an innovative global business hub to realise the vision of Manufacturing 2030.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our Manufacturing and Services sectors have traditionally been strong drivers of our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, weakening growth around the world, protracted supply disruptions and synchronised interest rate hikes have slowed down our manufacturing output recently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Given the large and diverse range of services that fall under the umbrella of the Services sector, the Government should pay attention to equitable growth across different service industries in addition to the sector as a whole.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How have our Manufacturing and Services sectors performed over the past year and what is the Government doing to develop the sector and create good jobs given rapid changes in product cycles and consumer behaviour?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Singapore has also been a leader in financial services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But other developing economies are growing these capabilities and will vie for the pie at lower costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are the growth and/or emerging industries and how can our firms seize opportunities in these areas?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, the global economy continues to be challenged with inflationary pressures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To stay competitive, Singapore needs to remain attractive to global investors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Global companies choose to invest in Singapore for our skilled labour, as seen in our Manufacturing and Services sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We have also focused on developing our local companies in these sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How have our Manufacturing and Services sectors performed?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In order for our local companies to remain competitive, they need to innovate and stay up to date with technological developments to create more efficient processes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With rising costs of operations, businesses will need support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Amidst global uncertainties, in the past year, we saw retrenchment and unemployment levels go up as businesses restructured their operations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Some workers might be at risk of redundancy and retrenchment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Businesses need to transform and build capabilities in order to create better jobs and remain attractive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While reskilling is important for workers to transition to more relevant jobs, there needs to be alignment of jobs in demand and training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What steps is the Government taking to develop the sector further to create good jobs in these sectors?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Good growth will create good jobs and sustainable businesses, and keep our economy resilient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What is the progress of the strategies of Singapore Economy 2030?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What are the growth and emerging sectors and how can businesses seize opportunities in these areas?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The refresh of ITMs aimed to better support companies in research, innovation and digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: They also set out to help SMEs by providing avenues for partnerships and better position companies for global opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can MTI share more details on how companies are doing and will be able to benefit from these ITMs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The objective of the refreshed ITMs is to encourage the use of Industry 4.0 technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How are companies transforming and leveraging digital and tech solutions?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How has the Government invested to transform and groom companies to adopt new solutions to remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These are now undergoing a refresh and complementary industries have also been clustered to encourage synergies between them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister provide an update on when the remaining refreshed ITMs will be launched?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister be able to share some insights into the effectiveness of the EDG in supporting businesses' transformation?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, while it is important for the Government to support businesses as they transform, it is also important to ensure that they do not become reliant on Government support.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government had put in significant resources to ensure that companies remain afloat during the pandemic, like the Job Support Scheme and Jobs Growth Initiative.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These schemes have since tapered off, but other schemes continue to provide funding to companies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When such businesses eventually face the risks of going under as Government schemes ceases or are tightened, there is a risk that the directors of these companies who had guaranteed loans may become personally liable and face bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Ministry consider measures to assist such individuals, as they are also victims of the pandemic, albeit belatedly suffering the effects.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As businesses transform, there may arise a need or opportunities for mergers and acquisitions (M&A).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The EDG currently supports the planning, assessment or potential mergers and acquisitions and post-M&A integration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, the biggest cost in M&A is in the actual work done to close and effect the M&A, including drafting the M&A contract – but this is specifically not allowed under EDG.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider extending EDG to support this as well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, building up advanced manufacturing capabilities is important for a country in order to remain competitive and successful in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Advanced manufacturing capabilities can contribute to economic growth by driving innovation, creating new products and services and increasing productivity and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This can lead to new business opportunities, job creation and increased competitiveness in the global market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: These capabilities drive technological advancement by enabling the development of new materials and production techniques.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This can also help to enhance a country's reputation as a leader in technological innovation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: It is critical for national security as these capabilities enable the production of key components and systems that are essential for defense and other critical applications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: For environmental sustainability, many new materials and advanced process are required to develop new products that contribute to environmental sustainability, enabling the production of more efficient and environmentally friendly products and reducing waste and emissions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Today, there are significant potential for growth and innovation for robotics and space.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Robotics can be used to automate production processes, increase efficiency and enhance quality control while space manufacturing can enable the production of advanced materials and components that are critical for space exploration and other applications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: These sectors will drive significant technological advancement as new products and services are developed and new materials and production techniques are used.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, how are we building our manufacturing capabilities for the future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, developing innovative capabilities is essential for the progress and relevance of the enterprise as well as for the collective ecosystem of the industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: There are many downstream benefits such as better trained manpower, competitive learning and more rapid adoption of technology as well as sharing of best practices and collaboration for the joint development of innovative technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Innovation is a key driver of economic growth and enterprises play a critical role in driving innovation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: By developing new products, services and processes, enterprise can create new markets, attract investment and create jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: In a globalised economy, enterprises that are more innovative are better able to compete on a global stage.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: By investing in innovation, enterprises can gain a competitive edge and contribute to the country's overall competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Innovation can also lead to increased productivity and efficiency, which can help to reduce costs and increase profits.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This can help enterprises to reinvest in their businesses, create new opportunities and contribute to the country's economic growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Innovative enterprise are more able to contribute to social progress by developing products and services that meet the needs of a growing and diverse population.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: They can help to improve access to education, healthcare and other critical services and create new opportunities for individuals and communities, especially in the area of employment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: How is the Government supporting enterprises in growing their innovative capabilities?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: The need for SMEs to embark on or continue their digitalisation journey is an urgent one.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These decisive commitments made in last 12 months should now translate to decisive actions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have seen sustainability efforts gather pace across Government agencies as well as large corporations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: According to UOB's SME Outlook Study in 2022, whilst three in five of Singapore's SMEs believe in the importance of incorporating sustainability practices, they face challenges in implementation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is urgent that we support our SMEs to take action to stay competitive and relevant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies are increasingly subjected to tighter sustainability reporting and regulations, particularly those with trading partners such as the EU, which have placed higher standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As more trading partners follow similar measures in meeting their own goals of net zero by 2050, our businesses will face growing pressures to adapt or face obsolescence.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critical that the Government supports industry to achieve a better understanding of the impact of a low-carbon future on their business and help them with the know-how and innovations that are available to make the green transition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They also need to make provisions for the carbon tax hike.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, companies have pointed out that the financing terms, which are intended to fund green transition, actually do not go far enough to spur adoption.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A Harvard Business Review report argued that whilst climate change mitigation efforts have been front and centre, more efforts must be dedicated to climate adaptation to help people, animals and plants survive because of the rising climate volatility.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Equipping the Singaporean workforce to take on jobs in the green economy must be a key priority.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As countries compete for green talents to meet Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) needs in the coming years, Singapore must both attract the best of sustainability as well as develop our own capabilities to nurture our pool of talent to take up green jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can Singaporeans receive the necessary training and credentials to secure green jobs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, oil and gas prices have been on a rollercoaster for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The COVID-19 demand crash, followed by the supply collapse caused by the Ukrainian war, plunged the world into an energy crisis which threatened countries with blackouts and freezing winters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Given the inherent volatility in energy production, supply and trading today, it is reassuring to hear our long-term plans to accelerate solar deployment, work with regional partners to develop regional power grids, import low-carbon electricity by 2035 and explore new alternative sources of energy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is encouraging that our National Hydrogen Strategy anticipates that hydrogen could supply up to half of power needs by 2050.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, the ordinary Singaporean and company would be equally concerned with the shorter-term affordability of electricity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: An update on the status and timelines of the consultation to enhance the regulatory regime for electricity retailers would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will Singapore safeguard our energy security and advance our energy transition despite our physical constraints and at the same time, balance the green transition?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How are we preparing to deal with increased volatility in the global energy markets?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is a small country with limited natural resources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Our energy needs are mostly imported, with few options for renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Most of Singapore's energy is generated by natural gas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Lowering our carbon emissions while ensuring our energy security and reliability is a challenge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In Budget 2023, Deputy Prime Minister Wong shared that Singapore is working towards the transition to solar energy and cleaner energy sources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: He also mentioned working with our neighbours to develop regional power grids.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It is important for our transition to alternative sources of energy to be a gradual one.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Our current sources of renewable energy are not sufficient to support all households and businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Even in resource-rich countries, the switch to renewable energy is not immediate and takes a few years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While more research is being conducted for more viable approaches to renewable energy, we will need to educate and prepare households and businesses for this switch to greener energy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For businesses in particular, the adoption of renewable energy options might incur greater operational costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is the Government investing to build Singapore's energy security to enable reliable and affordable sources of energy for businesses in line with our economic goals and environmental needs?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Faced with the need to keep prices low, countries are stockpiling energy and going back to coal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If this continues, it will be a vicious cycle, putting the planet's net-zero transition in jeopardy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The notion that energy security has to be secured at the expense of energy transition is a false one.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, this dilemma is an existential one that could erode our competitive position in the world economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Businesses are citing energy prices as one of the main drivers of business cost in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, other geographies are luring industrial investments with cheap energy price, and luring clean energy investments by providing very attractive tax credits for producing clean energy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, we have put solar panels all over many of our HDB blocks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how many of the solar panels are actually in operation today?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister also provide an update on Singapore's efforts to enhance our energy security and accelerate our energy transition, including driving energy efficiency, deployment of solar energy, development of emerging low carbon technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) and the import of renewable energy?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, decarbonisation is a generation defining business opportunities and our Singaporean companies are well-positioned to lead the way.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to the UOB SME Outlook Study 2022 Report, many SMEs understood the importance of sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need Enterprise Singapore to provide more assistance to SMEs so that they know how to measure emissions as many MNCs buyers have started to request their SME suppliers to furnish their carbon emission data.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the quantifiable aims of the Enterprise Sustainability Programme (ESP)?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does Enterprise Singapore promote this ESP to the 290,000 SMEs in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understood that many business consultants help to promote these Government schemes to the SMEs and assist these SMEs with the application of grants or reimbursements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These consultants' earnings are predicated on the loan amounts approved or amounts of grant received by the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If a particular scheme's approval process is lengthy or if there is no certainty that the grant can be approved after a huge amount of capital expenditure is incurred, the business consultants will only promote more straight-forward schemes, like Enterprise Financing Scheme, and not the ESP nor the Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also hope that Enterprise Singapore can process the reimbursements according to the mini project milestones completed so that these SMEs' cash flow constraints can be alleviated.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, how can more support be provided to the small accounting and auditing practices which provide sustainability accounting or assurance services to the SMEs?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Sustainability reporting has been gaining traction and more large corporations are publishing their sustainability reports to both meet regulatory needs and also to show commitment to climate goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Government planning to help SMEs in this shift towards greater accountability towards their carbon emissions to ensure they are able to meet the carbon accounting requirements of large corporations?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How long will these allowances be used for, and how will they affect the effectiveness of tourrevised carbon tax for incentivising decarbonisation?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is building a robust green talent pipeline in Government, industry and academia, as part of the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Green jobs ensure Singapore's long-term economic resilience and provide important social values.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: However, business costs have been increasing due to persistent inflationary pressures and other economic challenges.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: What are the Government's efforts to increase the awareness and accessibility of sustainability-related information, knowledge base and opportunities to support our businesses and workforce in the green transition.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government ensure sufficient green jobs and green growth opportunities for Singaporeans in the coming decades?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government help businesses embark on sustainability initiatives while reducing costs?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: There is a high demand for talent to field green jobs and greening jobs, but there is a significant gap in supply.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: There is a need for a more urgent agenda in green skilling that addresses these gaps.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Existing skilling efforts must be sharpened and accelerated.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The green skilling agenda must address gaps in green technical skills including deep engineering skills and supply chain skills, and move from awareness building to application orientation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can the Minister provide an update on how Singapore will develop the skills needed for a green economy in its workforce?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: I mentioned during the Budget debate that I am glad that the Government continues to encourage SMEs to look towards the longer term to transform and capture opportunities in the new economy, even as they are focused on overcoming near-term challenges.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: A key thrust I raised was about helping our SMEs develop Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) capabilities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: SMEs must adopt greener practices in their service and products, as well as measure, track and report their own carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Such measurement is not easy to do but is essential to stay relevant in tomorrow's green supply chain.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Beyond internal transformation, SMEs should venture out to pursue green prospects.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: For example, countries in the region are boosting electric vehicle (EV) initiatives.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This means opportunities for Singapore SMEs with capital and know-how. to help fellow businesses in the region to accelerate their green transition.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: I am glad that existing schemes, such as the Energy Efficiency Grant for the food and retail sectors, are retained.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Nonetheless, while these two sectors presumably consume more energy, I hope more SMEs across sectors can be included as all local businesses should be brought onto the green journey.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: The reality is that SMEs, especially smaller ones, may not know how or where to start.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In a nascent and growing market where standards have yet to achieve global consensus, there are opportunities for Singapore and our businesses to lead in the development of a credible regulatory framework and standards for carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: These efforts will help establish Singapore as a growing and leading green hub, leveraging on and furthering our status as a trusted international centre for professional services.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: To this end, can MTI share more on how businesses, including SMEs and the service sector, can play an expanded role, as part of plans to establish Singapore as an international green hub?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, to achieve our target of net zero emissions by 2050 will require all in Singapore to work together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Businesses are important stakeholders in our green transition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To make the transition will involve adoption of innovative measures and technology for businesses to be more sustainable and efficient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Often, this means that businesses will have to incur more costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: However, businesses are already facing increasing costs of operations and labour.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It is projected that these costs will continue to increase in 2023.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As we work towards decarbonisation, what are the Government's key measures to support businesses in the green transition?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How will the Government make it viable for businesses to embark on sustainability initiatives to reduce cost?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What support can be given to businesses to address current business costs pressures as they make the investments for the transition?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Being able to report their carbon emissions will increasingly become a requirement for doing business in many countries as well as with larger companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: SMEs may struggle to account for and report their carbon emissions if they are unable to deal with such costs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I want to record my appreciation to all my fellow workers in the power and gas industry for their tireless efforts to keep and ensure our lights on and the gas keeps flowing for our homes and businesses at all times, with or without COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our fellow workers regularly face brunt from the public whenever price hike is announced.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: When we, as workers, do not even have control over the price.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our strong tripartism model also involves having regular discussions with the Energy Market Authority (EMA) led by their CEO.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, prior to today, my fellow members have been pestering me for any recognition or even monetary awards from the Government, just like our healthcare workers, for their efforts to ensure highly reliable electricity and gas supplies during the COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We all know our hospitals are equipped with many highly sophisticated machines and needs highly reliable electricity and gas supplies for them to operate efficiently.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Have we ever imagined how it will turn out if we have power failure that would have failed the machines in hospitals during the COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our power and gas industry workforce is not as large as that in the healthcare industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, it would not burn a big hole in MTI's pockets to reward us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the workers in this industry have gone through and overcome many changes and challenges together.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our next big thing is getting our fellow workers ready for new skill sets required for the new energy solutions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Calling and rallying workers to attend training is never an easy feat.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In 2018, when SP Group embarked on Project Fusion, which meant future skills in everyone, my fellow union leaders and me, were given sarcastic remarks and bombarded by members and workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, we believed in this project as it was meant to prepare our workforce for the job roles of tomorrow and the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The training focuses on technological and technical fronts.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With such focus, it will result in higher value-add jobs and meaningful careers leading to better wages, work prospects and welfare.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, management reciprocated by revising their wages after certain periods into their new job roles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We will not stop here but will continue to press on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is City Energy, previously known as CityGas, who have decided to expand their business and move into new energy solutions, like green hydrogen and electric vehicles charging.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In order to prepare for this transformation, both the union and the management formed company training committees, followed by rallying and re-energising their workers in order to develop a strategically adept and proficient workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: UPAGE leaders will press on to advocate for our members' rights and long-term employability, in an efficient and a productive way.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: So, would the Minister for Trade and Industry who takes care of the energy industry, please do not disappoint us.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Some TACs are more able to play this role, while others, to be honest, are simply social clubs or talk shops, and yet others are plagued by internal politics and personal agendas and do not have much in terms of services to their members.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This could achieve two objectives: first to encourage TACs to level up in a structured manner and second, to help the other tripartite partners identify TACs that can play a bigger role in industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: These certified TACs could then be engaged by the Government to carry out such roles as administering industry-specific schemes and grants, and/or taking the lead in certain appropriate initiatives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: My second question, Sir, is a follow-up to a point I made in my Budget debate speech.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The key tripartite partner at the national level representing businesses is the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: On the MTI's pro-enterprise panel and other initiatives, the key business representative is the Singapore Business Federation (SBF).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The demands of the new workforce have seen a pivotal shift.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Businesses also need to be on the constant lookout for opportunities in overseas markets to diversify.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And this particularly affects our SMEs which comprise the vast majority and backbone of our economy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is where trade associations and chambers of commerce (TACs) have important roles to play.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over the years, especially through our history, TACs, such as SNEF and the Singapore Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) have been instrumental in the development of Singapore's business landscape by catalysing the building of capabilities in companies, especially SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their efforts in galvanising businesses to gain early mover advantages in then-emerging markets and capitalising from the digital transformation wave is what enabled Singapore to enjoy its status as a key business hub in the region.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In more recent years, TACs have also played their part in supporting a stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the success of the CDC Voucher scheme would not have been possible without the support from TACs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This clearly illustrates the vital role that TACs play in helping Singapore and its businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can our TACs magnify their roles in rallying industries and guiding businesses to overcome and emerge stronger from challenges?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we enable our TACs to better serve their members better?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: TACs can also work with its partners to provide more overseas work opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As mentioned in my earlier Budget speech, overseas work experiences are highly valued by our younger people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the extensive linkages enjoyed by our TACs across the globe, more can be done in terms of partnerships between companies to open up secondment programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, what are the resources that TACs can tap on to strengthen their internal leadership development and training?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Critical to a TAC's proper functioning is a strong secretariat because TACs' leadership are mostly comprised of business leaders contributing on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry could look into expanding the public sector's secondment or attachment schemes to TACs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such arrangements would be of mutual benefit to both TACs and the public sector with the exchange of skillsets and providing our people with broadened viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Another way to ensure a larger talent pool for TACs could be through establishing structured internship opportunities between our institutes of higher learn (IHLs) and TACs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There may also be scope to look into improving training for current employees of TACs to ensure that skillsets remain updated and relevant vis-a-vis the issues to be tackled by TACs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the Ministry can consider funding TACs to assist Singaporean businesses to expand overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the progress?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While businesses must continue to capture opportunities in big markets, such as China and India, more must be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, businesses must act fast to gain a first-mover advantage in emerging markets, such as Africa or Latin America.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Is the Ministry considering expanding on programmes, such as GlobalConnect@SBF to other TACs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as President of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Budget debate speech, I highlighted the need to strengthen consumer protection, particularly in our current inflationary environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, I would like to propose how we can do so in three areas.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, we should mandate prepayment protection for sectors which collect large sums of prepayments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, mandatory prepayment protection is already practised in some sectors, such as private education and massage establishments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This was a 24% increase from the $520,000 in losses reported by consumers in 2021.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Renovation contractors collect large sums of monies upfront, yet the industry lacks mandatory prepayment protection.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This places homeowners at significant risk, should anything adverse happen to the contractor.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, CASE accredits renovation contractors under the CaseTrust mark.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministry to expand mandatory prepayment protection to this industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, we should mandate a cooling-off period for the beauty industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, the laws already provide for a mandatory cooling-off period for certain industries, such as insurance and direct sales.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Complaints on pressure sales tactics and misleading and false claims account for 25% of beauty-related complaints received by CASE in 2022.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A mandatory cooling-off period will address the problem of pressure sales tactics by giving consumers sufficient time to consider or reconsider their purchases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If they do not wish to proceed with their beauty packages, they have the right to cancel and to obtain a refund.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, we should mandate seller verification on e-marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Last November, it was reported that a consumer bought an automated laundry rack on a major e-marketplace, only to receive a piece of cardboard and some clothes hangers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unfortunately, such scams are only the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mandating seller verification for e-commerce will ensure accountability of sellers for their product listings, reduce the risks of scams and aid resolution of consumer disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, let me first thank Members for your comments, suggestions and your views.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After more than three years of fighting the COVID-19 virus, we have now arrived at DORSCON Green.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Economic activities have largely resumed, and life has more or less returned to normal.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I must record my thanks and appreciation to our workers who have kept our economy going and our essential services flowing during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But even as we emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic, new challenges surfaced.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war compounded the supply chain disruptions triggered by COVID-19, driving up prices of energy, food and almost everything else.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Global inflation soared, which led many countries to tighten their monetary policies, causing the global economy to slow down.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore felt the effects of these global developments keenly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how the Singapore economy performed in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Outward-oriented industries, such as electronics, chemicals, and finance and insurance, were affected by weaker external demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, as countries emerged reopened their borders, the strong recovery in air travel and international arrivals have given a boost to our aviation- and tourism-related sectors, as well as consumer-facing sectors, such as retail trade and food and beverages (F&B) services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The professional services sector also benefitted from the lifting of travel restrictions, as businesses could better service and engage their customers overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nominal median gross monthly income for resident full-time workers grew by 8.3% in the same period.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After taking into account inflation, real median income grew by 2.0%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While higher wages add to the costs for businesses, the key is to ensure that productivity increases to support higher wages.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In this way, both businesses and workers will benefit.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Growth in the major advanced economies, such as the US and Europe, will slow amidst tightening financial conditions, which will crimp consumption and investment spending.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The possibility of recessions in these economies cannot be ruled out.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the upside, Asian economies are expected to continue growing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Southeast Asian economies will benefit from the ongoing recovery in domestic and tourism demand, while China's reopening is likely to provide some lift to global demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Global supply chains have recovered from the worst effects of the pandemic, but they continue to be affected by the Russia-Ukraine war and reshaped by efforts to re-shore or "friend-shore" operations and production.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a result, transport and logistics costs are likely to remain elevated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Several Members highlighted that businesses are having difficulties managing rising costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Derrick Goh and Mr Shawn Huang asked how the Government will assist businesses in overcoming these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
